analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $5.50 an hour and automatically increases it with inflation each year.
analysis.headline: A bill to raise the minimum wage to $5.50 and index it to inflation, with 50 House Democrats cosponsoring, never received a vote and died in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage to $5.50 an hour in 1994 and then automatically raised it every year after that, tying it to the cost of living the same way Social Security benefits are adjusted. Today the minimum wage only goes up when Congress votes to raise it, so its buying power slowly erodes between raises; this bill would have ended that cycle. It was introduced by Independent Rep. Bernie Sanders and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers earning at or near the federal minimum wage would see their pay rise to $5.50 an hour in 1994, and beginning in 1995 the wage would automatically rise each year with inflation, using the same cost-of-living formula Social Security benefits use, so their purchasing power would no longer erode between acts of Congress.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage to $5.50 an hour effective after December 30, 1993, a substantial increase for workers then earning the federal minimum.

Automatically adjusts the minimum wage each year for inflation using the same cost-of-living formula that applies to Social Security benefits, ending the pattern of the wage losing value between infrequent acts of Congress.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that pay minimum wage—especially restaurants, retail, and other labor-intensive employers—would bear higher payroll costs, and some of that cost would likely pass through to consumers in higher prices.

drawbacks.text: The $5.50 wage floor and automatic annual increases would raise labor costs for small businesses and labor-intensive employers, and economists disagree about how much of that cost would come back as reduced hours, fewer entry-level jobs, or higher prices rather than lower profits.

Hard-wiring annual inflation increases into law removes the flexibility to pause raises during a recession, which is one reason Congress has historically adjusted the minimum wage only in discrete steps.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and targeted: a higher wage floor for the lowest-paid workers, plus automatic inflation adjustments that would have kept it from quietly losing value. The main cost is higher payroll expenses for minimum-wage employers, some of which could show up as prices or reduced entry-level hiring—the standard trade-off debate over any minimum wage increase. Indexing to the Social Security formula is a well-tested mechanism, not an experiment. On balance, the bill would have transferred income from lower-wage employers and their customers to low-wage workers, and its automatic indexing addressed a real problem: Congress has repeatedly let the minimum wage erode for years before acting.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, then sent to a subcommittee, and it sat there with no markup and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on January 27, 1993, with Reps. Sabo and Owens as original sponsors, to raise the minimum wage to $5.50 and index it to inflation.

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor on the day it was introduced, and on February 11, 1993 it was sent further down to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, Occupational Health and Safety.
Fifty House Democrats cosponsored the bill, all from the Democratic side of the aisle, but the full committee never took it up and no floor vote ever happened.
Sanders spoke about the bill on the House floor on April 29, 1993, but that was the bill's last recorded action before the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay minimum wage, especially in restaurants and retail, were better off because the bill never advanced—the $5.50 wage floor and automatic inflation increases never took effect. Minimum-wage workers saw no change from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor in April 1993.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor leadership
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 27, 1993, and never reported it out; it was sent to a subcommittee and no vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was entirely from the Democratic side—50 House Democrats plus the Independent sponsor—with no Republicans cosponsoring, and the Democratic-controlled committee never moved the bill.

industries.note: Restaurants and fast food are the largest employers of minimum-wage workers, so a $5.50 floor with automatic annual increases would directly raise their labor costs. Their interest in keeping the wage floor lower runs against the wage gains workers would receive.

Retail and other labor-intensive service businesses employing many minimum-wage workers would face higher payroll costs under the higher floor and annual indexing. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against the workers it would have raised pay for.
